item.title: Randomization Inference for Dynamic Causal Effects in Short Panels with Autoregressive Instruments
item.description: arXiv:2610.19075v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: I study randomization inference for dynamic causal effects in panels with many units and few periods when treatment is endogenous and an instrument is as good as randomly assigned only through the innovations of a first-order autoregressive assignment mechanism with unknown persistence. The persistence is a nuisance parameter in two senses: it determines which weighted average of heterogeneous causal effects the instrumented local projection estimand measures, and it governs the randomization distribution of any statistic built from the instrument. I propose tests that never estimate it. For each candidate value the innovations are recovered, rerandomized under a group that leaves their joint law invariant, and a randomization p-value is formed; the reported p-value is the supremum over candidate values or over an exact confidence set. Under a sharp null on the path of lag-specific effects the tests have level at most $\alpha$ for every persistence in finite samples, including the unit root, and the supremum is a maximum over finitely many points. Under a weak null on the heterogeneity-weighted estimand a studentized version is uniformly asymptotically valid.
item.dc:creator: Pedro Picchetti

item.title: Propensity score with factor loadings: evaluating the effect of the Paris Agreement on the returns of European stocks
item.description: arXiv:2507.08764v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Factor models for longitudinal data, where policy adoption is unconfounded with respect to a low-dimensional set of latent factor loadings, have become increasingly popular for causal inference. Most existing approaches, however, rely on a causal finite-sample approach or computationally intensive methods, limiting their applicability and external validity. In this paper, we propose a novel method for panel causal inference within a super-population framework, based on inverse propensity score weighting, where the propensity score is a function of latent factor loadings. The approach relaxes the traditional restrictive assumptions of causal panel methods, while offering advantages in terms of causal interpretability, policy relevance, and computational efficiency. Under standard assumptions, we develop a three-step estimation procedure for the ATT and derive its large-sample properties using M-estimation theory. Simulation results show that the proposed estimator remains reliable across a variety of designs, including settings with misspecified factor structure and weakly dependent errors. We apply the method to assess the causal effect of the Paris Agreement - a policy aimed at fostering the transition to a low-carbon economy - on European stock returns. Our empirical results suggest a statistically significant and negative short-run effect on the stock returns of firms that demonstrate a strong commitment to sustainability.
item.dc:creator: Angelo Forino, Andrea Mercatanti, Giacomo Morelli

item.title: Two Gaussians, Too Many: A bootstrap-based approach to assess identifiability in non-Gaussian structural vector autoregressions
item.description: arXiv:2607.17275v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Normality pre-tests on reduced-form innovations cannot detect whether two or more underlying structural shocks are Gaussian, and hence cannot detect a failure of identification in non-Gaussian SVARs. We propose a bootstrap-based approach that reveals such a failure. Under the null of valid identification and certain regularity conditions, the conditional bootstrap distribution of the maximum likelihood estimator of the impact matrix is asymptotically normal, so the diagnostic reduces to a normality test on the bootstrap replications. The impact-matrix estimator remains consistent and asymptotically normal when one shock is Gaussian and its shape parameter lies on the boundary of the parameter space, so the diagnostic is valid across the entire null hypothesis. When the number of bootstrap replications and the sample size diverge jointly at an appropriate rate, the test statistic, conditional on the data, is asymptotically pivotal. This implies that conditioning on this diagnostic does not induce pre-testing bias asymptotically. In simulations with Normal-inverse Gaussian shocks, the multivariate diagnostic is close to its nominal size under the null, its power against an additional Gaussian shock increases with the sample size, and its univariate version localizes the failure in large samples. Based on the estimates of a SVAR in the macroeconomic and financial uncertainty literature, we demonstrate its potential as a practical, robust tool for assessing non-Gaussian identification.
item.dc:creator: Paritosh Shankarrao Junare

item.title: Heterogeneous Policy Effects in Comparative Case Studies with Treated-Unit Microdata
item.description: arXiv:2609.28678v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This article develops an identification framework for heterogeneous policy effects when individual-level data are available only in the treated jurisdiction. The framework combines outcome changes from repeated cross-sections within that jurisdiction with a population-average effect identified from aggregate panel data. Under conditional relative parallel trends and overlap, this information identifies subgroup effects standardized to the treated jurisdiction's overall post-treatment covariate distribution, but generally not effects averaged over each subgroup's own distribution. I establish how these subgroup-average effects can nevertheless be recovered using covariate-specific aggregate effects or additional pretreatment observations under assumptions about the evolution of untreated trends. Simulations and an application to the Massachusetts health reform illustrate the framework.
item.dc:creator: Carl Bonander

item.title: Vine Copula VAR:From Recursive Margins to Joint Forecast Inference
item.description: arXiv:2610.07589v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Joint-event forecasts combine an estimated dependence model with current marginal forecasts. Retaining historical transforms at the marginal fits available when each outcome arrived creates overlapping estimation errors. We derive their joint influence with the terminal estimates in a stable Vine Copula VAR with normal innovation margins and a fixed, correctly specified Gaussian or positive Clayton vine. An intercept identity and the stable VAR filter reduce the historical correction to harmonically weighted innovation moments. Terminal slope uncertainty remains in the forecast gradient. A feasible covariance estimator yields asymptotically valid repeated-sample intervals for fixed one-sided event probabilities at the realized forecast state. A same-family terminal refit provides the efficiency comparison. Retaining dated transforms adds a positive semidefinite limiting covariance term, whose event-level cost depends on dependence sensitivity and forecast-state leverage. Monte Carlo comparisons show a small accuracy cost of retaining the transforms and a larger inferential role for current marginal estimation. Allowing Clayton dependence improves downside forecasts relative to Gaussian dependence under each transform rule. A fourteen-variable U.S. real-time forecasting application and simulations with twenty and fifty variables illustrate feasible joint-event estimation and analytic inference for fixed-depth vines.
item.dc:creator: Hunter Ng, Yubo Tao

item.title: Relative Bias Under Imperfect Identification in Observational Causal Inference
item.description: arXiv:2507.23743v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: To conduct causal inference in observational settings, researchers must rely on certain identifying assumptions. In practice, these assumptions are unlikely to hold exactly. This paper considers the bias of selection-on-observables, instrumental variables, and proximal inference estimates under violations of their identifying assumptions. We develop bias expressions for IV and proximal inference that show how violations of their respective assumptions are amplified by any unmeasured confounding in the outcome variable. We propose a set of sensitivity tools that quantify the sensitivity of different identification strategies, and an augmented bias contour plot visualizes the relationship between these strategies. We argue that the act of choosing an identification strategy implicitly expresses a belief about the degree of violations that must be present in alternative identification strategies. Even when researchers intend to conduct an IV or proximal analysis, a sensitivity analysis comparing different identification strategies can help to better understand the implications of each set of assumptions. Throughout, we compare the different approaches on a re-analysis of the impact of state surveillance on the incidence of protest in Communist Poland.
item.dc:creator: Melody Huang, Cory McCartan

item.title: Bootstrap inference in factor-augmented regressions with weak factors
item.description: arXiv:2510.00947v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this paper, we develop bootstrap methods for factor-augmented regressions with potentially weak common components, allowing signal eigenvalues to diverge at heterogeneous rates $N^{\alpha_k}$, where $0<\alpha_k\leq1$, $k=1,\ldots,r$. The regression estimator targets a rotation of the latent parameter vector that may be data dependent, while factor estimation can induce asymptotic bias. The proposed procedure directly constructs the rotation-specific target in the bootstrap world, avoiding the additional randomness induced by existing bootstrap methods. Bootstrap distributional validity is established for two data-dependent targets and a signal-dependent population target, where studentization provides asymptotically pivotal statistics for both analytical and bootstrap bias-corrected estimators. The analysis also distinguishes distributional approximation relative to a data-dependent target from inference on fixed population restrictions and introduces a bootstrap diagnostic for rotation uncertainty (RU) when signal eigenvalues are close. Monte Carlo experiments show improved bias correction, gains from bootstrap distributional approximation, and demonstrate that inference distortions from small signal eigengaps dissipate quickly with $T$ for fixed targets, in contrast to the persistent distortions under random rotations. An application to excess bond return predictability illustrates the practical importance of bootstrap distributional approximation and rotation uncertainty for inference on individual factor coefficients.
item.dc:creator: Peiyun Jiang, Takashi Yamagata

item.title: Random sets from the perspective of metric statistics
item.description: arXiv:2511.13440v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Since the seminal work by Beresteanu and Molinari(2008), the random set theory and related inference methods have been widely applied in partially identified econometric models. Meanwhile, there is an emerging field in statistics for studying random objects in metric spaces, called metric statistics. This paper clarifies a relationship between two fundamental concepts in these literatures, the Aumann and Fr\'echet means, and presents some applications of metric statistics to econometric problems involving random sets.
item.dc:creator: Daisuke Kurisu, Yuta Okamoto, Taisuke Otsu

item.title: Beyond Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) Accelerators: Directed Evidence for Adaptive Sustainability Portfolios
item.description: arXiv:2601.20875v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Governments and development partners often seek Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) "accelerators" whose progress can propagate gains across human well-being, institutions, resources, and environmental priorities. Such claims require evidence on direction, timing, robustness, and trade-offs, not only network connectivity. We map directed SDG interdependence using a balanced panel of 114 countries observed annually from 2000 to 2024. Because the goal series are persistent, trending, and cross-sectionally dependent, we combine Dumitrescu-Hurlin panel Granger non-causality tests on first-differenced series with false-discovery control across 272 directed goal pairs, and panel local projections with Driscoll-Kraay standard errors for 31 theory-derived indicator linkages. We find 84 directed linkages after correction: 40 synergies and 44 trade-offs. This dense structure does not support a universal accelerator. Driver-receiver rankings are fragile across lag orders, centrality metrics, bootstrap resampling, and alternative dependence controls; only peace and strong institutions as a net receiver and poverty reduction as an effect-size-weighted driver are distinguishable in the bootstrap screen. Two local-projection pathways are supported, both leading to lower child mortality, and the education-child-health association is corroborated in independent World Development Indicators data across 183 countries. The policy implication is not to abandon SDG integration, but to replace fixed global accelerator rankings with adaptive portfolios built around supported, time-lagged linkages and monitored constituent indicators.
item.dc:creator: Md Muhtasim Munif Fahim, Md Jahid Hasan Imran, Md. Naim Molla, Luknath Debnath, Tonmoy Shil, Ehsanul Bashar Pranto, Md Mostafizur Rahman Likhon, Md Shafin Sanyan Saad, Md. Rezaul Karim

item.title: Robustifying Empirical Bayes
item.description: arXiv:2603.00704v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Two strategies are explored for robustifying classical denoising procedures for the Gaussian sequence model. First, the Hodges and Lehmann (1952) restricted Bayes approach is used to reduce sensitivity to the specification of the initial prior distribution. Second, alternatives to the Gaussian noise assumption are explored. In both cases proposals of Huber (1964) and Mallows (1978) play a crucial role.
item.dc:creator: Roger Koenker, Jiaying Gu
